extracted.intended_audience: editors, publishers, and staff of peer-reviewed medical journals; authors and reviewers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for defining, declaring, disclosing, and managing conflicts of interest (COI) in peer-reviewed medical journals, aimed at journal editors, reviewers, and authors. Covers types of competing interests, procedural rules for disclosure, responsibilities of participants, and options for handling COI when identified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of conflict of interest (COI)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Conflict of interest (COI) exists when there is a divergence between an individual’s private interests (competing interests) and his or her responsibilities to scientific and publishing activities such that a reasonable observer might wonder if the individual’s behavior or judgment was motivated by considerations of his or her competing interests."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: COI affects authors, reviewers, and editors and is especially problematic when not apparent; the appearance of COI alone can erode trust and credibility even if no wrongdoing occurred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journals must have and publish COI policies
rubrics_metrics.description: "Every peer-reviewed medical journal (herein 'Journal') should have its own COI policies for authors, reviewers, and editors."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policies should be readily accessible (published with instructions for authors). The Editorial COI Policy that addresses editor COI should be published as well. The statement summarizes main elements and offers examples/options for disclosure and management.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publish journal-specific definition and scope of COI
rubrics_metrics.description: "Journals should publish their own definition of COI."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definition should specify who is covered (authors, reviewers, editors), what responsibilities are affected (academic honesty, unbiased conduct, integrity of decisions), and which parts of the publication process are included (submission, peer review, editorial decisions, communications).

rubrics_metrics.name: Financial ties constitute a competing interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Financial competing interest exists when a participant has received or expects to receive money (or other financial benefits such as patents or stocks), gifts, or services that may influence work related to a specific publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: payment for research, stock/stock options, honoraria, consultation fees, advisory board service, patents/pending patents, positions funded by companies selling products related to the work. Financial COI may be past or expected in future; includes 'insider trading' (use of privileged information). Other funders (government, charities, professional groups) may also create competing interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Academic commitments/intellectual passion as COI
rubrics_metrics.description: Participants' strong beliefs or reputational commitments to particular explanations, methods, or ideas can bias their conduct of research or their review of competing work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E.g., an established investigator who defends a paradigm may judge challenging new work harshly; investigators in the same field may find fault with competing teams. Editors should be aware of such commitments and potential influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal relationships as COI
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal relationships with family, friends, enemies, competitors, or colleagues can pose conflicts of interest for participants in the publication process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E.g., a reviewer who has been working colleagues with authors may have difficulty providing an unbiased review; similar concerns apply for strong bonds to family members.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political or religious beliefs as COI
rubrics_metrics.description: Strong political positions, agendas, party affiliations, or religious convictions may pose a COI if the publication affirms or challenges those views.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such nonfinancial competing interests should be recognized and managed where relevant to the manuscript content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional affiliations as COI
rubrics_metrics.description: A COI exists when a participant is directly affiliated with an institution that may have a position or interest in a publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: employment by a company that manufactures a studied product, institutions holding patents on devices, laboratories funded by private donors with potential stakes, institutions sponsoring trials, or institutions engaged in related litigation. Even apparently neutral institutions (universities, hospitals) may have interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specify what, how, to whom, and when to declare
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals’ policies must take into consideration: What COI must be declared, how, to whom and when?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be as specific as possible about operational definitions and the kinds of competing interests to be declared. Provide clear instructions for making declarations and indicate that journals may ask follow-up questions or clarifications (e.g., request details about future monetary gains or how independence was maintained in funded labs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Require written declarations as condition of review
rubrics_metrics.description: "All declarations about COI should be requested in writing as a condition of reviewing a manuscript."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask in a way that maximizes likelihood authors/reviewers will report their COIs related to the manuscript; journals may follow up for clarification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journals should set standards/timeframes for financial COI
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no universally accepted standard for the degree or timeframe of financial COI; journals should publish their own standards for financial COI, including expiry (e.g., only declare COI within last five years).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judgments about risk of bias depend on amount, recency, expectation of future reward, and services provided in return; be explicit about the journal's timeframe and thresholds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Management of COI depends on disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: "Managing COI depends on disclosure because it is not possible to routinely monitor or investigate whether competing interests are present."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclosure should state facts relevant to COI; assertions of integrity alone are not sufficient. Because routine monitoring is impractical, accurate and timely disclosure is critical to effective management.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences and investigations for undeclared COI
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals should state steps editors will take if competing interests surface after submission or publication, including investigation and possible action if allegations are true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigations should be completed as quickly as reasonably possible; if COI surfaces after publication, journals may publish investigation results as a correction and ask authors to explain publicly why COI was not revealed earlier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be transparent about COIs that bar consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals must be transparent about COI situations that, if present, will result in a manuscript not being considered further.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: some journals exclude authors with competing financial interests from writing narrative (not systematic) reviews because bias is harder for readers to detect; internal editorial rules that disqualify submissions should be articulated publicly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publish COI disclosures with the publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals should publish all relevant COI disclosures with the publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Additional management options include: not considering a manuscript further; excluding those with COI from the process (reviewer or editor); abstaining from decisions where COI might arise; investigation by impartial observers; and including links to institutional COI information when available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ask authors to declare funder role and participation
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should explicitly state funding sources and whether the organization that funded the research participated in collection, analyses, interpretation, or reporting of results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals should publish all COIs (or their absence) reported by authors relevant to the manuscript; policies should extend beyond financial COI to other competing interests that might affect conduct or reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewers must disclose COI and be removed if conflicted
rubrics_metrics.description: "Reviewers should be asked if they have a COI with the content or authors of a manuscript. If they do, they should be removed from the review process."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generally avoid reviewers from the same institution as the authors unless the institution is so large that authors and reviewers are not working colleagues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editors must recuse and should not make decisions when conflicted
rubrics_metrics.description: "Editors should not make any editorial decisions or be involved in the editorial process if they have or a close family member has a COI (financial or otherwise) in a particular manuscript submitted to their journal."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a manuscript is from an editor's own department or institution (especially small ones), have explicit pre-established policies for managing this. When editors submit their own work, a colleague in the office should manage the manuscript and the editor/author should recuse from discussion/decisions. Listing editors' competing interests on the journal website is an option though not standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Educate and raise awareness about COI
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals have a responsibility to raise awareness and educate the research community about COI.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One recommended practice is to ask investigators and reviewers reflective questions such as: 'if my competing interest becomes known to others later, would I feel defensive or would others in the publication process, readers or the public think I was hiding or misleading them?'

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide mechanisms to seek additional information or clarification
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals may ask additional questions or seek clarification about declarations (for example, details about future monetary gains or written details about how independence was maintained).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This enables journals to better assess the significance and manageability of disclosed competing interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use institutional COI disclosures/e-links
rubrics_metrics.description: Some research institutions provide COI information on their websites; journals should routinely ask authors to disclose such e-links as part of their COI disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Including institutional COI documentation can assist transparency and the journal's evaluation of potential institutional conflicts.
